extracted.intended_audience: general readers; philanthropists; historians of philanthropy and civic benefaction
extracted.subtask_description: Autobiographical narrative outlining Andrew Carnegie's principles, practices, and aims for charitable giving — including targeting of recipients, gift design (endowments, pensions, public parks), coordination with other funders, and philanthropy for peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting philanthropy to smaller institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our chief universities, such as Harvard and Columbia, with five to ten thousand students, were large enough; that further growth was undesirable; that the smaller institutions (the colleges especially) were in greater need of help and that it would be a better use of surplus wealth to aid them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer directing surplus wealth toward smaller colleges and institutions rather than expanding already-large universities; focus on where marginal dollars produce greater benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperate with other foundations and funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Coöperation was soon found to be much to our mutual advantage, and we now work in unison (referring to coordination with Mr. Rockefeller's General Education Board).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate giving with other major funders to avoid duplication or undesirable results; formal or informal cooperation improves outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use named gifts to commemorate friends and exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts often named for friends (e.g., Conway Hall at Dickinson College named for Moncure D. Conway; the Stanton Chair of Economics at Kenyon College founded in memory of Edwin M. Stanton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming chairs, libraries, or buildings after individuals both honors them and links philanthropy to personal relationships; examples illustrate practice and social recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematize giving with formal application and graduated grants
rubrics_metrics.description: A printed schedule requiring answers to many questions has now to be filled and returned before action is taken... the department is now perfectly systematized and works admirably because we graduate the gift according to the size of the church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement formal application procedures and scale grant sizes to recipient capacity so that distribution is orderly, equitable, and administrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require recipient cost‑sharing to ensure responsible expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: In requiring the congregation to pay one half of the cost of better instruments, there is assurance of needed and reasonable expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demanding a proportionate financial contribution from beneficiaries (e.g., half the organ cost) secures their commitment, discourages waste, and ensures appropriate use of funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design private pension funds to provide modest, dignified support
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all my work of a philanthropic character, my private pension fund gives me the highest and noblest return... Modest sums insure this freedom. Not one person have I ever placed upon the pension list that did not fully deserve assistance. It is a real roll of honor and mutual affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pension schemes should provide modest but sufficient support to ensure comfortable old age, preserve beneficiaries' dignity, and avoid publicity; beneficiaries should be selected as 'worthy' by known criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer personal knowledge when selecting pension beneficiaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The Railroad Pension Fund ... benefits the worthy railroad men who served under me when I was superintendent on the Pennsylvania... Most of the men beneficiaries of the fund I have known personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, use personal acquaintance or direct knowledge of candidates as a selection criterion for pension/support funds to ensure trustworthiness and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentatious personal provisions for individual recipients; trust trustees' discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker Washington suggested changing a clause providing a large sum for future support to 'only suitable provision' and 'I'll trust the trustees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure gifts so they do not embarrass recipients or create misconceived impressions; allow trustees discretion to set appropriate personal provisions rather than rigid, large sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public gifts should elevate everyday life — 'sweetness and light' — especially for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust deed wording: 'To bring into the monotonous lives of the toiling masses of Dunfermline, more "of sweetness and light," to give to them—especially the young—some charm, some happiness, some elevating conditions of life...' If this be the fruit of your labors, you will have succeeded; if not, you will have failed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess public gifts by their capacity to uplift everyday life, with special emphasis on benefits for children and young people; success is measured by lasting improvement in community well‑being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use endowments (invested bonds) to secure long‑term community benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: When they heard that half a million sterling in bonds, bearing five per cent interest, was also to go to them for the benefit of Dunfermline, they were surprised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide perpetual or long-term funding via endowments (bonds or similar instruments) to ensure sustained maintenance and programming for public gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design public gifts for active community use and events
rubrics_metrics.description: The children's yearly gala day, the flower shows and the daily use of the Park by the people are surprising. The Glen now attracts people from neighboring towns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan parks and public amenities to host recurring events and daily use, thereby maximizing social impact and encouraging regional visitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund peace and international arbitration institutions when solicited and in cooperation with governments
rubrics_metrics.description: When Andrew D. White and Mr. Holls... suggested that I offer the funds needed for a Temple of Peace at The Hague... the Dutch Government did make application... the draft for a million and a half is kept as a memento.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support institutions for peace (e.g., Peace Palace) and arbitration, but act in response to legitimate governmental or institutional requests rather than presumptuously imposing large projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use philanthropic hosting and social gatherings strategically to foster reconciliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral: If you wish to play peace-maker, seat adversaries next each other where they must begin by being civil... It certainly is often the way to peace to invite your adversary to dinner...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage dinners, seating plans, and social events to encourage civil engagement between adversaries; social proximity can reduce misunderstandings and promote reconciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose recipients devoted to uplift rather than self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Every institution in which I became interested, revealed many men and women devoting their time and thought, not to 'miserable aims that end with self,' but to high ideals which mean the relief and uplift of their less fortunate brethren.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select organizations and individuals who demonstrate selfless commitment to public uplift; prioritize high‑minded aims over projects that primarily serve private interests.
